title: Drupal site settings over JSON:API, per consumer
description: Decoupled Settings serves the site and theme config Drupal already holds over JSON:API, and lets every frontend override just the values it needs. Four years ago I guessed the answer would be Consumers plus theme settings. Turns out it was.

content.html:
In April 2022 I wrote about decoupling configuration with Config Pages. It opened with a complaint:

While the Drupal JSON:API still doesn't provide anyway [sic] to access basic site configuration, there are many ways it can be done...

And it ended with a guess at where I'd go next:

One of my future experiments with Druxt will be to look at the options of using the Drupal Consumers module alongside Drupal theme settings as a solution.

That experiment is now a module. Decoupled Settings reads the site and theme configuration Drupal already holds, serves an allowlisted slice of it over JSON:API, and lets every frontend override just the values it needs. It went up on Drupal.org this week.

Core's JSON:API is an entity API. Content entities and config entities alike, so node types, image styles and views are all in there. What it has never exposed is simple configuration, and there's a good argument that it shouldn't by default, because plenty of what sits in system.site is nobody's business.

But a decoupled frontend still needs the boring stuff:

  • The site name, for the document title
  • The slogan
  • The logo and the favicon
  • The front page path, so the router knows what "home" means

Every decoupled build I've worked on has solved that itself, and mostly solved it by keeping a second copy of the site name somewhere.

paragraphs.title: Isn't that what Config Pages is for?

content.html:
Partly, and I'm not walking away from it. Config Pages is still on my sites and I'd still reach for it tomorrow.

What it's for is settings you invent. The 2022 post was about an app being fed configuration data from Drupal, and that's the job: define a Config Page type, add the fields the app needs, done. Nothing has changed there.

Where it gets awkward is settings Drupal already stores. Model the site name as a field on a Config Page and the site name exists in two places, and something has to keep them in step, and sooner or later something won't.
So the module doesn't store settings. It reads them from the config objects that already hold them, and a consumer stores only what it changes.

content.alt: The per-consumer overrides form for a consumer named Partner Portal, filtered to system.site. Columns are Setting, Inherited value, Override and Value for this consumer. system.site:name and system.site:slogan are ticked and overridden to 'Partner Portal' and 'Same code, different consumer'; langcode, page.403, page.404 and page.front are unticked and inherited.
content.caption: Filtered to system.site, and trimmed to the first six rows. The full form on a stock install lists 23 settings, two of them overridden here.

content.html:
Tick a setting, give it a value, and that consumer sees your value. Leave it unticked and it keeps following the site, so overriding one frontend's name doesn't freeze its front page path.

An override set to an empty value is still a value. If a frontend shouldn't display a slogan at all, tick it and leave the field blank, and that's what it gets. Clearing the override is a separate action, and that's the one that restores inheritance. Every settings system I've built before this collapsed those two together and I've regretted it every time.

One thing worth knowing before you plan a deployment around it: the exposure list is configuration and travels with drush cim, but the per-consumer overrides are stored on the consumer entity, so they're content. They live in the database and they don't move between environments with your config.
Only the config objects you list, and within those, only the keys typed config schema declares. On install that's system.site plus the active theme.

content.alt: The Decoupled Settings configuration form: an Exposed configuration list containing system.site, a checkbox to expose the active theme settings, an Excluded settings box containing system.site:mail, and a 'What a frontend will read' table listing config object, setting and global value.
content.caption: Same crop caveat: filtered to system.site and trimmed to seven rows, so the theme's fourteen keys aren't in shot.

content.html:
That preview table is the part I'd actually use. It shows what a frontend gets right now, unsaved changes included, which means a key that's missing for lack of schema is visible rather than silent.

It also shows you how much you're handing over. The default on a stock Drupal 11 install is 23 keys, not the handful you might picture: admin_compact_mode, weight_select_max, the theme's features block and its base_primary_color all come along. Read the table and trim what you don't want.

Both of system.site's email keys are excluded by default, which is the sort of thing worth checking rather than assuming: the exclusion list is the only thing standing between a schema-declared key and any frontend that asked for its config object.

content.title: Abbreviated: 7 of the 23 keys, otherwise as returned

content.html:
A few things about that response, each of which you would otherwise learn the hard way.

olivero.settings is the machine name of whatever theme that site runs. It is not a fixed part of the contract, so don't hardcode it in a client.

consumerId is the consumer's client ID, not its label. Mine is labelled "Partner Portal" and its client ID is partner_frontend.

And a name that matches nothing isn't an error. You get HTTP 200, the global values, and "consumer": null. That is the documented behaviour, but it means a typo in a CI variable ships the wrong branding with a green build, so check the consumer field before you trust the payload. The endpoint is read-only, incidentally: POST gets you a 405.

Reading needs the Read decoupled settings permission, and it isn't granted to anonymous on install. The module does nothing at all until you've decided whether these values are public.

It's one switch for the whole endpoint, though, and that's worth understanding before you plan around it. Naming a consumer selects whose overrides you get. It isn't a second authorisation step. So anyone holding the permission can read any consumer's settings by naming it, and client IDs are guessable. Per-consumer overrides are not per-consumer secrets, which matters if you're running frontends for two different clients out of one backend.

Serving public basics to anonymous and protected extras to authenticated apps from the same site isn't expressible yet either. Per-consumer include and exclude lists are the designed answer and they aren't built.

paragraphs.title: Caching, and the two ways to name yourself

content.html:
A consumer identifies itself with the consumerId query parameter or the X-Consumer-ID header, and they behave differently enough that it's worth choosing between them.

The query parameter caches normally, one page cache entry per URL, and it's the one I'd reach for. The header path is deliberately kept out of Drupal's internal page cache, because that cache keys on URL alone and would happily serve one consumer's settings to the next, so it costs a full bootstrap on every request.

Responses do collect the config cache tags of every object that contributed, so an editor changing the site name invalidates them with nobody writing a hook. That's internal to Drupal, though. On the wire the response is Cache-Control: must-revalidate, no-cache, private with a Vary: X-Consumer-ID, so nothing is cached at a CDN unless you set one up yourself, and if you do, check it honours that header before you go live.

There's a companion Druxt module in review that does the frontend half. At build time it identifies itself as a consumer, reads the endpoint, and bakes the result into the build, title and favicon included. Run the same repository twice with two different consumer IDs and you get two differently branded sites out of it.

Baking it in at build time is the trade being made: the artifact ends up with no runtime dependency on Drupal, and the price is that a settings change means a rebuild. If you'd rather have live values, fetch the endpoint at runtime and the cache tags start earning their keep.

Worth being precise about how far that goes. A consumer gets its own name, slogan, front page and branding assets. Menus, regions, layouts and per-market content are all still yours to solve.

Multilingual is half done, and I'd rather say which half. Exposed values follow interface language negotiation, so a request to a language-prefixed URL returns that language's translated config. A per-consumer override replaces the value in every language at once, and there's no per-language override. So you can translate your site name, or you can brand it per consumer, but not both.

The 2022 post said I found the other side of that coin more interesting, one frontend against many backends. Four years on, it's this one people keep asking me for.

It's 1.0.0-beta2, and it's a beta for a reason. Before I'd call it stable I want per-consumer include and exclude lists either built or deliberately deferred, a real consumer of this API that isn't my own Druxt module, and some soak time on sites that aren't mine.

That has consequences worth saying out loud. Drupal's security advisory policy only covers stable releases, so a beta has no security team backing it. And if you adopt now you become that second consumer, which means your integration is the thing most likely to force a change in the response shape before 1.0. I'd rather tell you that than have you find out.

On the other side of the ledger: 108 tests and 492 assertions across unit, kernel and functional coverage. The GitLab CI pipeline on drupalcode.org runs those against Drupal 11 and came back green across all eight jobs on its first run, which never happens. Drupal 10 gets its own matrix legs on GitHub, and they pass too, so the version shim is exercised rather than merely declared.
If any of that is useful to you, the beta is out now:

The include and exclude lists, then File (Field) Paths, which I said was next up last time and still is. This one just kept nagging at me until I wrote it.

If you're running decoupled Drupal already, how are you getting the site name into your frontend today? I'd like to know, while the API shape is still soft enough to change.
